## Search method v012

Define X and Y exactly, including requested entity unit, exclusions, subtypes, group-membership rules and effective dates. Start sequentially with broad X-only, Y-only and conjunction searches. Add a compact relation ledger only when sources show that a predicate is recorded on a different entity unit: for example a qualifying group, credited work, event, institution or named record linked to the requested entity. Record the intermediate entity, the explicit relationship, source, applicable date and missing edge. Treat shared names as identity questions, not relationships. After the baseline, ask whether either frontier systematically hides eligible entities behind such a relationship. If so, substitute one source-grounded bridge probe for a normal discovery probe: retrieve the qualifying intermediate entity's explicit recipients, named members, creators or other eligibility-relevant roster, and bring newly identified requested-unit entities into the frontier. A confirmed find may supply a bridge lead, but do not infer that its associates qualify. Expand only relationships permitted by the hunt, at most one intermediate entity between the requested entity and each predicate; do not crawl arbitrary collaborators or biographies. Select one promising bridge at a time and check at most three new identities before expanding further. Prefer paths that establish one predicate for several new identities and leave only one inexpensive check each. Stop a bridge family after two probes add neither source-backed candidates nor useful missing-edge evidence; return to ordinary opposite-frontier or residual-scope discovery. No bridge is mandatory when the source structure provides no justification. Run small discovery/check rounds prioritized by total resolution cost, with a genuine neglected-scope probe each round. Check only unresolved predicates and identity edges, preserving established facts. Group membership or work association does not automatically transfer an award or status: require the hunt's exact qualifying relationship and date. Silence remains unresolved. After two unproductive discovery searches, prohibit synonymous conjunction searches and try an untested sibling or unrestricted parent on the opposite frontier, or an evidenced untested relation path. Reserve at least 35% of initial funds for checks; stop discovery when pending checks consume the remainder. Perform up to three affordable final residual probes on distinct untested restrictions or relation paths, stopping after two without candidates or useful evidence. Extract explicit identities rather than guessed associates, and preserve the source supporting each edge. ## SiftText

SiftText is persistent memory across chats.

Entry: /Users/jack/sifttext/nodes/5e565245-14fe-406c-977c-cf94a9be246b/node.md
Retrieval guide: /Users/jack/sifttext/nodes/526ed0f5-4e5d-42b3-9e3f-b7ad429f2df8/node.md

At the start of every new chat, unless I say not to use SiftText, before any other tool call:
1. Run `sifttext instructions`.
2. Read the Entry above and follow it, plus any `agent-instructions` the command returns.
3. Before retrieving knowledge, read the Retrieval guide above, do not search first.

## Tooling policy

- Never directly invoke `python`, `python3`, `pip`, or `pip3` unless explicitly instructed by the human.
- Use `uv` for all agent-initiated Python work:
  - Python execution: `uv run python ...`
  - Scripts and tests: `uv run ...`
  - Throwaway dependencies: `uv run --with <package> ...`
  - Python CLI tools: `uvx <tool>`
  - Durable project dependencies: use the project's appropriate `uv` command and preserve its lockfile.
- For non-Python probing or testing with unavailable tools:
  - One executable: `nix run nixpkgs#<package> -- <args>`
  - Temporary environment: `nix shell nixpkgs#<package> ... --command <command>`
- Nix environments are temporary, but downloaded store paths may remain cached until garbage collection.
- If a Nix dependency becomes useful for recurring or future work, tell the human and suggest adding it to the appropriate durable Nix configuration (such as a project flake/dev shell, Home Manager, or nix-darwin configuration). Do not make that durable change unless asked.

</addendum>

# All Nobel Prizes in Physics

The Nobel Prize in Physics has been awarded 120 times to 231 Nobel Prize laureates between 1901 and 2026. John Bardeen is the only laureate who has been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics twice, in 1956 and 1972. This means that a total of 230 individuals have received the Nobel Prize in Physics. # All Nobel Prizes in Physics

The Nobel Prize in Physics has been awarded 120 times to 231 Nobel Prize laureates between 1901 and 2026. John Bardeen is the only laureate who has been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics twice, in 1956 and 1972. This means that a total of 230 individuals have received the Nobel Prize in Physics. # All Nobel Prizes in Physics

The Nobel Prize in Physics has been awarded 120 times to 231 Nobel Prize laureates between 1901 and 2026. John Bardeen is the only laureate who has been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics twice, in 1956 and 1972. This means that a total of 230 individuals have received the Nobel Prize in Physics. ### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2026](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2026/summary/)

[Francis Halzen](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2026/halzen/facts/)

> “for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2025](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2025/summary/)

[John Clarke](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2025/clarke/facts/), [Michel H. Devoret](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2025/devoret/facts/) and [John M. Martinis](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2025/martinis/facts/)

> “for the discovery of macroscopic quantum mechanical tunnelling and energy quantisation in an electric circuit”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2024](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2024/summary/)

[John J. Hopfield](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2024/hopfield/facts/) and [Geoffrey Hinton](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2024/hinton/facts/)

> “for foundational discoveries and inventions that enable machine learning with artificial neural networks”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2023](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2023/summary/)

[Pierre Agostini](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2023/agostini/facts/), [Ferenc Krausz](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2023/krausz/facts/) and [Anne L’Huillier](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2023/lhuillier/facts/)

> “for experimental methods that generate attosecond pulses of light for the study of electron dynamics in matter”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2022](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2022/summary/)

[Alain Aspect](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2022/aspect/facts/), [John Clauser](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2022/clauser/facts/) and [Anton Zeilinger](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2022/zeilinger/facts/)

> “for experiments with entangled photons, establishing the violation of Bell inequalities and pioneering quantum information science”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2021](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2021/summary/)

> “for groundbreaking contributions to our understanding of complex physical systems”

[Syukuro Manabe](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2021/manabe/facts/) and [Klaus Hasselmann](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2021/hasselmann/facts/)

> “for the physical modelling of Earth’s climate, quantifying variability and reliably predicting global warming”

[Giorgio Parisi](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2021/parisi/facts/)

> “for the discovery of the interplay of disorder and fluctuations in physical systems from atomic to planetary scales”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2020](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2020/summary/)

[Roger Penrose](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2020/penrose/facts/)

> “for the discovery that black hole formation is a robust prediction of the general theory of relativity”

[Reinhard Genzel](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2020/genzel/facts/) and [Andrea Ghez](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2020/ghez/facts/)

> “for the discovery of a supermassive compact object at the centre of our galaxy”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2019](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2019/summary/)

> “for contributions to our understanding of the evolution of the universe and Earth’s place in the cosmos”

[James Peebles](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2019/peebles/facts/)

> “for theoretical discoveries in physical cosmology”

[Michel Mayor](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2019/mayor/facts/) and [Didier Queloz](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2019/queloz/facts/)

> “for the discovery of an exoplanet orbiting a solar-type star”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2018](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2018/summary/)

> “for groundbreaking inventions in the field of laser physics”

[Arthur Ashkin](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2018/ashkin/facts/)

> “for the optical tweezers and their application to biological systems”

[Gérard Mourou](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2018/mourou/facts/) and [Donna Strickland](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2018/strickland/facts/)

> “for their method of generating high-intensity, ultra-short optical pulses”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2017](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2017/summary/)

[Rainer Weiss](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2017/weiss/facts/), [Barry C. Barish](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2017/barish/facts/) and [Kip S. Thorne](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2017/thorne/facts/)

# All Nobel Prizes in Physics

The Nobel Prize in Physics has been awarded 120 times to 231 Nobel Prize laureates between 1901 and 2026. John Bardeen is the only laureate who has been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics twice, in 1956 and 1972. This means that a total of 230 individuals have received the Nobel Prize in Physics. [Eric Cornell](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2001/cornell/facts/), [Wolfgang Ketterle](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2001/ketterle/facts/) and [Carl Wieman](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2001/wieman/facts/)

> “for the achievement of Bose-Einstein condensation in dilute gases of alkali atoms, and for early fundamental studies of the properties of the condensates”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2000](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2000/summary/)

> “for basic work on information and communication technology”

[Zhores Alferov](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2000/alferov/facts/) and [Herbert Kroemer](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2000/kroemer/facts/)

> “for developing semiconductor heterostructures used in high-speed- and opto-electronics”

[Jack Kilby](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2000/kilby/facts/)

> “for his part in the invention of the integrated circuit”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 1999](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1999/summary/)

[Gerardus 't Hooft](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1999/thooft/facts/) and [Martinus J.G. Veltman](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1999/veltman/facts/)

> “for elucidating the quantum structure of electroweak interactions in physics”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 1998](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1998/summary/)

[Robert B. Laughlin](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1998/laughlin/facts/), [Horst L. Störmer](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1998/stormer/facts/) and [Daniel C. Tsui](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1998/tsui/facts/)

> “for their discovery of a new form of quantum fluid with fractionally charged excitations”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 1997](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1997/summary/)

[Steven Chu](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1997/chu/facts/), [Claude Cohen-Tannoudji](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1997/cohen-tannoudji/facts/) and [William D. Phillips](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1997/phillips/facts/)

> “for development of methods to cool and trap atoms with laser light”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 1996](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1996/summary/)

[David M. Lee](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1996/lee/facts/), [Douglas D. Osheroff](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1996/osheroff/facts/) and [Robert C. Richardson](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1996/richardson/facts/)

> “for their discovery of superfluidity in helium-3”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 1995](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1995/summary/)

> “for pioneering experimental contributions to lepton physics”

[Martin L. Perl](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1995/perl/facts/)

> “for the discovery of the tau lepton”

[Frederick Reines](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1995/reines/facts/)

> “for the detection of the neutrino”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 1994](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1994/summary/)

> “for pioneering contributions to the development of neutron scattering techniques for studies of condensed matter”

[Bertram N. Brockhouse](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1994/brockhouse/facts/)

> “for the development of neutron spectroscopy”

[Clifford G. Shull](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1994/shull/facts/)

> “for the development of the neutron diffraction technique”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 1993](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1993/summary/)

[Russell A. Hulse](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1993/hulse/facts/) and [Joseph H. Taylor Jr.](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1993/taylor/facts/)

> “for the discovery of a new type of pulsar, a discovery that has opened up new possibilities for the study of gravitation”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 1992](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1992/summary/)

[Georges Charpak](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1992/charpak/facts/)

> “for his invention and development of particle detectors, in particular the multiwire proportional chamber”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 1991](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1991/summary/)

[Pierre-Gilles de Gennes](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1991/gennes/facts/)

> “for discovering that methods developed for studying order phenomena in simple systems can be generalized to more complex forms of matter, in particular to liquid crystals and polymers”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 1990](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1990/summary/)

[Jerome I. Friedman](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1990/friedman/facts/), [Henry W. Kendall](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1990/kendall/facts/) and [Richard E. Taylor](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1990/taylor/facts/)

> “for their pioneering investigations concerning deep inelastic scattering of electrons on protons and bound neutrons, which have been of essential importance for the development of the quark model in particle physics”

Barkla ( Moon )

Named after Charles Glover Barkla - British physicist; Nobel laureate (1877-1944).

You are a web search agent. Follow your search method.

## Search method v012

Define X and Y exactly, including requested entity unit, exclusions, subtypes, group-membership rules and effective dates. Start sequentially with broad X-only, Y-only and conjunction searches. Maintain deduplicated frontiers, identity/evidence and scope ledgers as in v007: record accidental restrictions, derive a few source-backed sibling partitions, and never treat restricted success as parent-category coverage. Add a compact relation ledger only when sources show that a predicate is recorded on a different entity unit: for example a qualifying group, credited work, event, institution or named record linked to the requested entity. Record the intermediate entity, the explicit relationship, source, applicable date and missing edge. Treat shared names as identity questions, not relationships. After the baseline, ask whether either frontier systematically hides eligible entities behind such a relationship. If so, substitute one source-grounded bridge probe for a normal discovery probe: retrieve the qualifying intermediate entity's explicit recipients, named members, creators or other eligibility-relevant roster, and bring newly identified requested-unit entities into the frontier. A confirmed find may supply a bridge lead, but do not infer that its associates qualify. Expand only relationships permitted by the hunt, at most one intermediate entity between the requested entity and each predicate; do not crawl arbitrary collaborators or biographies. Select one promising bridge at a time and check at most three new identities before expanding further. Prefer paths that establish one predicate for several new identities and leave only one inexpensive check each. Stop a bridge family after two probes add neither source-backed candidates nor useful missing-edge evidence; return to ordinary opposite-frontier or residual-scope discovery. No bridge is mandatory when the source structure provides no justification. Run small discovery/check rounds prioritized by total resolution cost, with a genuine neglected-scope probe each round. Check only unresolved predicates and identity edges, preserving established facts. Group membership or work association does not automatically transfer an award or status: require the hunt's exact qualifying relationship and date. Silence remains unresolved. After two unproductive discovery searches, prohibit synonymous conjunction searches and try an untested sibling or unrestricted parent on the opposite frontier, or an evidenced untested relation path. Reserve at least 35% of initial funds for checks; stop discovery when pending checks consume the remainder. Perform up to three affordable final residual probes on distinct untested restrictions or relation paths, stopping after two without candidates or useful evidence. Submit only deduplicated entities with both predicates and every required identity or relationship edge supported.

### Routing policy
Default route: providers ['parallel'], tier default, 8 results per provider.
check_candidates route: ['parallel'].
Parallel alone, default tier, 8 results for baseline, bridge and residual discovery; 4 for exact missing-edge checks and check_candidates. Use verified intermediate-entity names and neutral relationship questions, not asserted eligibility. Price each candidate and query separately, including downstream relationship checks. No routine also variants, auto-routing or multi-provider requests. Escalate only promising ambiguous, conflicting or inaccessible individual cases to Exa alone with 4 results. At most one initial Exa discovery probe after genuinely different Parallel scope or relation partitions stagnate, continued only if it adds useful identities or evidence. Domain-filter targeted roster, credit or authoritative-record checks, not broad frontier coverage; relax failed filters. Publication-date filters apply only when publication date defines eligibility; check relationship and status effective dates in content.

### Fetch policy
Reuse cached evidence. Prefer fetching the specific roster, credit table, namesake origin or record section that can expose and support a missing relation edge. Inspect its entity unit, inclusion rules, dates and relevant pagination before treating it as covered. Extract explicit identities rather than guessed associates, and preserve the source supporting each edge. Fetch authoritative missing-predicate pages when needed; do not fetch every result or enumerate a whole institutional census. After a blocked or uninformative page, try one targeted alternate source. No acceptance based solely on a generated relationship summary or an uninspected plausible URL.

# All Nobel Prizes in Physics

The Nobel Prize in Physics has been awarded 120 times to 231 Nobel Prize laureates between 1901 and 2026. John Bardeen is the only laureate who has been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics twice, in 1956 and 1972. This means that a total of 230 individuals have received the Nobel Prize in Physics. ### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2026](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2026/summary/)

[Francis Halzen](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2026/halzen/facts/)

> “for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2025](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2025/summary/)

[John Clarke](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2025/clarke/facts/), [Michel H. Devoret](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2025/devoret/facts/) and [John M. Martinis](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2025/martinis/facts/)

> “for the discovery of macroscopic quantum mechanical tunnelling and energy quantisation in an electric circuit”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2024](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2024/summary/)

[John J. Hopfield](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2024/hopfield/facts/) and [Geoffrey Hinton](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2024/hinton/facts/)

> “for foundational discoveries and inventions that enable machine learning with artificial neural networks”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2023](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2023/summary/)

[Pierre Agostini](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2023/agostini/facts/), [Ferenc Krausz](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2023/krausz/facts/) and [Anne L’Huillier](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2023/lhuillier/facts/)

> “for experimental methods that generate attosecond pulses of light for the study of electron dynamics in matter”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2022](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2022/summary/)

[Alain Aspect](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2022/aspect/facts/), [John Clauser](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2022/clauser/facts/) and [Anton Zeilinger](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2022/zeilinger/facts/)

> “for experiments with entangled photons, establishing the violation of Bell inequalities and pioneering quantum information science”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2021](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2021/summary/)

> “for groundbreaking contributions to our understanding of complex physical systems”

[Syukuro Manabe](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2021/manabe/facts/) and [Klaus Hasselmann](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2021/hasselmann/facts/)

> “for the physical modelling of Earth’s climate, quantifying variability and reliably predicting global warming”

[Giorgio Parisi](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2021/parisi/facts/)

> “for the discovery of the interplay of disorder and fluctuations in physical systems from atomic to planetary scales”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2020](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2020/summary/)

[Roger Penrose](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2020/penrose/facts/)

> “for the discovery that black hole formation is a robust prediction of the general theory of relativity”

[Reinhard Genzel](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2020/genzel/facts/) and [Andrea Ghez](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2020/ghez/facts/)

> “for the discovery of a supermassive compact object at the centre of our galaxy”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2019](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2019/summary/)

> “for contributions to our understanding of the evolution of the universe and Earth’s place in the cosmos”

[James Peebles](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2019/peebles/facts/)

> “for theoretical discoveries in physical cosmology”

[Michel Mayor](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2019/mayor/facts/) and [Didier Queloz](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2019/queloz/facts/)

> “for the discovery of an exoplanet orbiting a solar-type star”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2018](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2018/summary/)

> “for groundbreaking inventions in the field of laser physics”

[Arthur Ashkin](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2018/ashkin/facts/)

> “for the optical tweezers and their application to biological systems”

[Gérard Mourou](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2018/mourou/facts/) and [Donna Strickland](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2018/strickland/facts/)

> “for their method of generating high-intensity, ultra-short optical pulses”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2017](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2017/summary/)

[Rainer Weiss](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2017/weiss/facts/), [Barry C. Barish](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2017/barish/facts/) and [Kip S. Thorne](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2017/thorne/facts/)

> “for decisive contributions to the LIGO detector and the observation of gravitational waves”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2016](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2016/summary/)

[David J. Thouless](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2016/thouless/facts/), [F. Duncan M. Haldane](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2016/haldane/facts/) and [J. Michael Kosterlitz](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2016/kosterlitz/facts/)

> “for theoretical discoveries of topological phase transitions and topological phases of matter”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2015](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2015/summary/)

[Takaaki Kajita](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2015/kajita/facts/) and [Arthur B. McDonald](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2015/mcdonald/facts/)

> “for the discovery of neutrino oscillations, which shows that neutrinos have mass”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2014](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2014/summary/)

[Isamu Akasaki](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2014/akasaki/facts/), [Hiroshi Amano](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2014/amano/facts/) and [Shuji Nakamura](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2014/nakamura/facts/)

> “for the invention of efficient blue light-emitting diodes which has enabled bright and energy-saving white light sources”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2013](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2013/summary/)

[François Englert](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2013/englert/facts/) and [Peter Higgs](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2013/higgs/facts/)

> “for the theoretical discovery of a mechanism that contributes to our understanding of the origin of mass of subatomic particles, and which recently was confirmed through the discovery of the predicted fundamental particle, by the ATLAS and CMS experiments at CERN's Large Hadron Collider”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2012](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2012/summary/)

[Serge Haroche](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2012/haroche/facts/) and [David J. Wineland](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2012/wineland/facts/)

> “for ground-breaking experimental methods that enable measuring and manipulation of individual quantum systems”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2011](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2011/summary/)

[Saul Perlmutter](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2011/perlmutter/facts/), [Brian P. Schmidt](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2011/schmidt/facts/) and [Adam G. Riess](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2011/riess/facts/)

> “for the discovery of the accelerating expansion of the Universe through observations of distant supernovae”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2010](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2010/summary/)

[Andre Geim](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2010/geim/facts/) and [Konstantin Novoselov](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2010/novoselov/facts/)

> “for groundbreaking experiments regarding the two-dimensional material graphene”

[Charles K. Kao](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2009/kao/facts/)

> “for groundbreaking achievements concerning the transmission of light in fibers for optical communication”

[Willard S. Boyle](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2009/boyle/facts/) and [George E. Smith](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2009/smith/facts/)

> “for the invention of an imaging semiconductor circuit - the CCD sensor”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2008](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2008/summary/)

[Yoichiro Nambu](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2008/nambu/facts/)

> “for the discovery of the mechanism of spontaneous broken symmetry in subatomic physics”

[Makoto Kobayashi](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2008/kobayashi/facts/) and [Toshihide Maskawa](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2008/maskawa/facts/)

> “for the discovery of the origin of the broken symmetry which predicts the existence of at least three families of quarks in nature”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2007](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2007/summary/)

[Albert Fert](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2007/fert/facts/) and [Peter Grünberg](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2007/grunberg/facts/)

[John C. Mather](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2006/mather/facts/) and [George F. Smoot](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2006/smoot/facts/)

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2005](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2005/summary/)

[John L. Hall](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2005/hall/facts/) and [Theodor W. Hänsch](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2005/hansch/facts/)

> “for their contributions to the development of laser-based precision spectroscopy, including the optical frequency comb technique”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2004](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2004/summary/)

[David J. Gross](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2004/gross/facts/), [H. David Politzer](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2004/politzer/facts/) and [Frank Wilczek](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2004/wilczek/facts/)

> “for the discovery of asymptotic freedom in the theory of the strong interaction”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2003](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2003/summary/)

[Alexei Abrikosov](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2003/abrikosov/facts/), [Vitaly L. Ginzburg](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2003/ginzburg/facts/) and [Anthony J. Leggett](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2003/leggett/facts/)

> “for pioneering contributions to the theory of superconductors and superfluids”

[Raymond Davis Jr.](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2002/davis/facts/) and [Masatoshi Koshiba](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2002/koshiba/facts/)

[Riccardo Giacconi](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2002/giacconi/facts/)

[Eric Cornell](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2001/cornell/facts/), [Wolfgang Ketterle](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2001/ketterle/facts/) and [Carl Wieman](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2001/wieman/facts/)

> “for basic work on information and communication technology”

[Zhores Alferov](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2000/alferov/facts/) and [Herbert Kroemer](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2000/kroemer/facts/)

[Jack Kilby](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2000/kilby/facts/)

[Gerardus 't Hooft](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1999/thooft/facts/) and [Martinus J.G. Veltman](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1999/veltman/facts/)

> “for elucidating the quantum structure of electroweak interactions in physics”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 1998](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1998/summary/)

[Robert B. Laughlin](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1998/laughlin/facts/), [Horst L. Störmer](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1998/stormer/facts/) and [Daniel C. Tsui](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1998/tsui/facts/)

[Steven Chu](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1997/chu/facts/), [Claude Cohen-Tannoudji](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1997/cohen-tannoudji/facts/) and [William D. Phillips](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1997/phillips/facts/)

[David M. Lee](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1996/lee/facts/), [Douglas D. Osheroff](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1996/osheroff/facts/) and [Robert C. Richardson](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1996/richardson/facts/)

> “for pioneering experimental contributions to lepton physics”

[Martin L. Perl](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1995/perl/facts/)

> “for the discovery of the tau lepton”

[Frederick Reines](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1995/reines/facts/)

> “for the detection of the neutrino”

> “for pioneering contributions to the development of neutron scattering techniques for studies of condensed matter”

[Bertram N. Brockhouse](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1994/brockhouse/facts/)

> “for the development of neutron spectroscopy”

[Clifford G. Shull](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1994/shull/facts/)

> “for the development of the neutron diffraction technique”

[Russell A. Hulse](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1993/hulse/facts/) and [Joseph H. Taylor Jr.](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1993/taylor/facts/)

[Georges Charpak](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1992/charpak/facts/)
